author: reek
body: The ocean model, drawn. `OceanModel` samples the surface at four points and prints them; four numbers are enough to check that a normal is unit and that foam appears where the Jacobian folds, and they are not enough to see whether the thing looks like water. This chapter evaluates the same model over a grid, projects the displaced points through a camera, and fills the triangles into the GOP framebuffer, so the output is an image rather than a reading.

author: reek
body: Nothing here changes the model. Every surface point still comes from `eval-surface` and every colour still comes from `shade-point`. What is added is a camera, a scanline filler, and distance haze.

author: reek
body: Three choices worth stating, because each had an alternative.

author: reek
body: The framebuffer is written directly with `poke-32` rather than through `Game chapter Rasterizer`. That chapter carries the same scanline math and is the obvious thing to cite, but its `Framebuf` is a `List Integer` and `fb-set` builds a fresh `Framebuf` record for every pixel it writes. On a heap with no collector that is a record per pixel for a quarter of a million pixels, to produce an intermediate that would then have to be copied into the framebuffer anyway. The filler below is the same algorithm without the copy or the garbage.

author: reek
body: There is no depth buffer. The grid is drawn one band at a time from the far edge toward the camera, which is a painter's ordering and is exact for a heightfield. Gerstner displacement can fold a crest over the trough in front of it, and where it does the near band wins by drawing later, which is the wrong answer for those pixels. It costs a few pixels at a crest lip and it saves sorting every triangle.

author: reek
body: The wave list is bound once in `opening` and threaded through every call. A list constant is rebuilt at each mention, so naming `ocean-waves` inside the per-vertex path would rebuild four `Wave` records for every vertex on the grid.

author: reek
body: The standing GOP surface codex-vm renders at 0xBF000000: one 32-bit XRGB pixel per cell, row-major, no pitch padding. A write outside the bounds is dropped rather than wrapped. The resolution here must match the `-gop-width` and `-gop-height` the machine is booted with; the sidecar in the README passes both.

author: reek
body: A vertical gradient, dark at the zenith and pale at the bottom, so the water has something to fog into and the image has a horizon. The water is drawn over the lower part of it.

author: reek
body: A look-at frame built from the eye the model already carries. Right is the cross product of world up with forward, which is what puts world +x on the right of the image for a camera looking along +z; up is then forward crossed with right. A point is projected by measuring it along the three axes and dividing the two lateral components by the forward one.

author: reek
body: Aerial perspective. Without it the grid ends in a hard line across the image where the last band stops, which reads as a cut sheet rather than a sea. Fogging the far water into the same colour the sky reaches at the horizon hides the edge for the same reason it does outdoors.

author: reek
body: One grid vertex: where the displaced surface point lands on screen, whether it is in front of the camera at all, and the colour the model shades it. Colour is carried per vertex and averaged per triangle, so a facet takes the mean of its three corners rather than one sample.

author: reek
body: The grid is shaped like the view frustum, not like a rectangle of water.

author: reek
body: A rectangular slab is the obvious thing to sample and it is wrong here, for a reason worth writing down because the picture it produces does not look like a domain problem. Fix the width and the near rows are as wide as the far ones while sitting a few units from the eye, so they project to thousands of pixels across and arrive as slivers spanning the screen, while the far rows shrink below a pixel and contribute nothing. The first render of this chapter was that image.

author: reek
body: Making each row's half-width proportional to its distance ahead of the eye gives every row roughly the same width on screen and every quad roughly the same screen area, which is where the samples are worth spending. The margin carries the row edges past the frame so the sides are covered.

author: reek
body: Rows are spaced quadratically in depth, so the near water, which fills most of the image, gets most of the rows.

author: reek
body: A frustum-shaped grid holds the screen density constant, which means the world-space spacing between samples grows without bound with distance. The far rows of this grid sit 4 units apart and the shortest wave in the set is 3.8 units long, so out there the wave field is sampled below its Nyquist rate. An undersampled sine does not fade out, it returns an arbitrary phase per vertex, and the model faithfully reports what those phases imply: gradients that are nonsense, a Jacobian that folds, and foam. The first frustum render came back 99 per cent foam-white for exactly this reason, and nothing was wrong with the model.

author: reek
body: So each row gets its own copy of the wave set with the waves it cannot resolve attenuated out. A wave is at full strength when its wavelength is four or more times the row spacing and gone by twice it, faded rather than dropped so that a wave does not pop as a row crosses the threshold. Amplitude and steepness are attenuated together, which keeps the crest sharpening in proportion to the height it sharpens.

author: reek
body: This is the same thing a mip-mapped displacement map does on a GPU, and the same thing an eye does: distant water is smooth because its small structure is below the resolution looking at it.

author: reek
body: Scanline fill of a screen triangle, sorted by y and swept in two halves across the long edge. The same shape as the one in `Game chapter Rasterizer`, writing pixels instead of building a framebuffer record.

author: reek
body: A facet is drawn only when all three of its corners are in front of the camera. A partially visible triangle is dropped rather than clipped: the grid starts well in front of the eye, so the only facets this discards are behind the camera entirely.

author: reek
body: The image is the deliverable, but a run that only paints tells you nothing on a terminal. These two counts are read back out of the framebuffer after the draw, and both are numbers that move when the render breaks: covered counts pixels that no longer hold the sky gradient their row was cleared to, so it goes to zero if the mesh fails to draw, and foam counts near-white pixels, which is the model's own Jacobian criterion arriving on screen.

author: reek
body: codex-vm captures the framebuffer on a timer while the guest is still running, so a program that draws and exits inside a second is already gone when the capture fires. The driver holds after drawing.

author: reek
body: The hold counts PIT ticks at cell 28672 rather than spinning a fixed number of iterations, so it is a duration and not a guess about how fast this machine retires instructions. The fuel cap is not decoration: on a machine booted with the timer disabled the tick never advances, and without the cap the hold would be permanent.

author: reek
body: In a run that takes a screenshot the capture ends the guest partway through this hold, so the last line the driver prints does not appear. That absence is the capture working.
